This was a Children, Young People and Education Committee meeting with a focus on higher and further education. It was mainly about questions on teacher training and teacher training for secondary school teachers in particular, focusing on the recruitment problem and the problem of those websites that offer to write essays for cash. The committee also discussed the issue of pensions, which was discussed by Kirsty Williams, Cabinet Secretary for Education, Eluned Morgan, Minister for Welsh Language and Lifelong Learning, and Huw Morris, who is the group director of skills, higher education and lifelong learning.

Suzy Davies AM asked about the problem of recruiting teachers into the 300 priority places, and Kirsty Williams AM answered that although they were in touch with their providers, they were not in a position to give figures for this year's intake for a couple of months. However, they had seen over recent years that they were only recruiting to about 65 per cent of those targets, which was a cataclysmic drop, and they had a job of work to do to understand and respond to those needs. They had put in place new incentives, both for people starting their course and then for teachers who complete their QTS after a year to try and address some of those issues.

According to Kirsty Williams, although they were in touch with their providers, they were not in a position to give figures for this year's intake for a couple of months, but what they had seen over recent years was that they were only recruiting to about 65 per cent of those targets. What they were doing was first of all making sure that their ITE provision was world class, so that Welsh centres were the place to go to train to be a teacher. They were also embarking on their first ever national ITE recruitment marketing exercise. They had initially done some work in the last year specifically targeting Welsh students in studying for priority subject degrees, e-mailing them, sending them materials to ask them to consider (1) becoming a teacher, and (2) crucially coming to do that training here in Wales.

Kirsty Williams did not believe that their action was enough because it was an international issue. The accreditation process, which was independent of the Government, demanded of ITE-providers that their provision would be able to meet the goals of their curriculum. Their curriculum was very clear about the equality of the language and the ability of our children, through all stages of their education journey, to be bilingual children. Therefore, it had to be a UK approach.

Hefin David thought that the Education Workforce Council was not accrediting the University of South Wales with the ability to deliver teacher training because they had made it clear that they expected very high standards in the ITE system and the accreditation process demanded ITE providers that their provision would be able to meet the goals of the curriculum. However, Kirsty Williams insisted that the process was independent of the Government and it was not appropriate for him to comment on that further.

From the very outset of the ITE reforms, Kirsty Williams had made it clear that he expected very high standards in their ITE system, and the accreditation process demanded of ITE providers that their provision would be able to meet the goals of the curriculum. The curriculum was very clear about the equality of the language and the ability of children, through all stages of their education journey, to be bilingual children. It was an international issue, and it would have an impact for what they do, but it was not for me to second-guess the judgment of previous Ministers who pursued this particular policy agenda.

Currently, with the current providers, there was a significant geographical spread. There were centres here in the south-east, there were centres in mid Wales, and in north Wales. Obviously, accessibility was an issue for them. Therefore, they responded with their part-time PGCE route, which actually would be location neutral, because they would be able to study that as a distance learner, and so they could remain in their community and undertake that course. So, if geographical disadvantage was stopping somebody from pursuing a career aspiration to qualify as a teacher, they would allow them to do that.

Hefin David asked if the Cabinet Secretary was in favor of more university mergers. Kirsty Williams AM said he was in favour of a healthy, strong and sustainable HE sector. He did not have a burning desire or a set policy to pursue mergers, but he did not intend to change that view. Hefin David also asked about the long-term sustainability of the University of South Wales, which was still agnostic on the matter. However, he did raise concerns about the Newport aspect, which had been somewhat denuded by the merger, and the amount of activity in the new Newport campus and elsewhere in Newport had been reduced.

Kirsty Williams did not have a formal policy for reconfiguration or mergers, but he was in favor of a healthy, strong and sustainable HE sector. He was all for universities and institutions working together, but there was no formal policy. These were autonomous institutions. If they saw that there was an advantage, then they would obviously have an interest in that and make sure that they were robust plans, but that was a matter for individual institutions. There was no pressure from the Government to pursue an agenda of mergers.

Kirsty Williams personally was not aware of any disadvantage to Cardiff Met, but he would recognise the position of staff and students caught up in those deliberations and those issues, which would have had a personal impact on them. In terms of the institution going forward, Kirsty Williams was really heartened by some of the really interesting collaborative work that Cardiff Met were interested in doing, and new partnerships and new collaborations between institutions, whether that be Cardiff Uni or local colleges, which was to be welcomed.

This was the Children, Young People and Education Committee's last formal meeting before the Senedd. It was mainly about the impact of the coronavirus pandemic on health and social services as they relate to children and young people in Wales. The meeting mainly covered questions from members, such as access to health services, mental health, childcare, substance misuse and vulnerable groups.

According to Vaughan Gething, the government still had seven-day-a-week crisis care, including those for children and young people, which was essential and not to be scaled down. Meanwhile, perinatal mental health services had not been stopped either, as they had also been looking at how that was provided on a phone or online basis where possible, because the same concerns existed about physical contact with people.

Vaughan Gething believed that children's mental health was a central concern and remained so for both the education minister and the health minister. They were working together with both health boards and their own knowledge and analytical services across the Government to both try to further understand what was and the difference, and that was a real point of concern for me. In all of the unknowns within this, the impact on mental health and well-being was absolutely one of them, because they were looking at how they then developed not just a recovery plan for the economy but an overall recovery plan around mental health, how we support people, and it would have to be informed by the understanding of what's happening when they got more engagement with families about the level of need, and then how they needed to think about that.

Sian Gwenllian asked about the capacity for CAMHS primary mental health services. Tracey Breheny said that there had been some movement around health boards, particularly where in the first phase of the epidemic the concentration was on in-patient provision, providing critical care, but the understanding was from the latest tool that they looked at last week, those staff were gradually not just returning to work from self-isolation or whatever, or from different parts of the system.

The group talked about the evaluations on the increasing suicide crimes during the COVID-19 and the long-term special care for the pregnant women. The first thing they did was to commission a review to be carried out with the current numbers of unexpected deaths that they had, so they were able to provide a report to understand where they were. The second thing they talked about was the evaluation on the mental health and well-being of children and young people, which they had commissioned a national advisory group to review the current, unexpected deaths during the start of the pandemic here in Wales, because they wanted to try to understand the wider concerns about the potential effects of the restrictions on the Mental Health and Well-Being of Children and young People, and if that was leading to a spike in suicide or not.

When talking about the evaluations on the increasing suicide crimes during the COVID-19 and the long-term special carefor the pregnant women, Lynne Neagle AM asked about the provision of crisis care. Vaughan Gething AM first made clear that mental health services, including those for children and young people, were essential services to be provided. They had built up those crisis care services over a period of time, and the last thing they wanted to see was to see them disappear during this period when there were well-understood concerns about emotional and mental health.

When discussing the long-term special care for the pregnant women, Lynne Neagle AM asked about the perinatal mental health service which had not been stopped either. Vaughan Gething AM explained that the service still absolutely exists and the government was still committed to it. However, he was concerned about the time frame because it was partly about the length and the extent.

According to Julie Morgan, the current Welsh Government definition and guidance around vulnerable children and young people included those with a social worker and with statements of special educational needs, and the most vulnerable of these should be prioritized. However, the coronavirus emergency opened up a whole new group of children that were not necessarily known to services but could still be vulnerable. Therefore, they had set out an expanded definition, which included discretion for local authorities to have some flexibility and to be able to offer a place for those who may be on the edge of receiving care and support if they were known to be vulnerable by the school or by family support services.

Julie Morgan thought it was difficult to monitor if there was not easy access to the children that they were referring to, and that's why they had been trying to encourage the vulnerable children to go into school or childcare settings. The monitoring system was carried out on a case-by-case basis, so every case that was known was being RAG rated and services were being linked to that.

Julie Morgan said that they had worked with the fostering organizations. They had had close communications with them, and they supported AFA Cymru to develop guidance for foster carers, and that guidance had been very strongly welcomed across the sector. They were also working with the third sector. The Fostering Network had extended its helpline hours, and Voices from Care had developed this particular offer of support for care leavers. The young people appeared to be more stable now and they had contact with.

According to Julie Morgan, the government had taken a strong line at the beginning that they weren't going to introduce easements in requirements to children's social services. However, they had commissioned a review to be carried out with the current numbers of unexpected deaths that they had, so they were able to provide a report to understand where they were. On the other hand, according to Suzy Davies, the children's rights impact assessments had not been done and the government was still concerned about the direct physical and mental health impact of lockdown restrictions.

When talking about the evaluations on the legitimacy of the children's rights, protection and demands, Julie Morgan mentioned that they were actually launching a survey of children. This was an online survey that they hoped would be going out to thousands of children, and they would get their response in terms of what were the important issues that had arisen for them. What they felt about what had happened during this period, what they wanted to do about the situation, and their views on the whole COVID-19 situation.

When discussing the evaluations on the legitimacy of the children's rights, protection and demands, Albert Heaney mentioned that they had not introduced any easements in relation to children's services legislation, which was really quite crucial for the Welsh context, because the standards that were in place did remain, so therefore there wouldn't have been a necessity for them to do a Children's rights impact assessment in the relation to the primary legislation. However, in terms of childcare and education, they were obviously looking at the provisions under the coronavirus Act to allow them to maybe ease some of the statutory requirements, and they were going to be undertaking a full suite of impact assessments on those. Obviously, they definitely would be looking at those impacts in the future.

The meeting was the first hybrid meeting of the House of Commons Special Committee on the COVID-19 Pandemic. Some members were participating via videoconference and some were participating in person. In the early days of the pandemic and the lockdown that followed, Canadians were told by the government that programs would be rolled out very quickly and that gaps and shortcomings would be changed as time went on. The opposition party argued that the Covid-19 crisis should not be used as an excuse to avoid presenting solutions to the missing and murdered indigenous women and girls committee, in particular by delaying action on the calls for justice. The focus had always been on the most vulnerable, first and foremost.

The opposition party and the Prime Minister commented about companies laying off workers in the midst of pandemic. The Prime Minister said that the government recognized that a number of organizations and companies were facing difficulties because of COVID-19, and they were supporting people all over the country through the wage subsidy program. However, the opposition party pointed out that certain companies and businesses had particularities that meant it was a little more difficult for them to qualify, so the government promised to continue to target companies and not innocent workers.

The issue of long-term care was brought up after the military report revealed the appalling conditions experienced by seniors in the care homes in Ontario. It was alleged that the for-profit model was failing the seniors and putting profits ahead of the well-being of seniors. The opposition party argued that the federal government should be held accountable for its support for the provinces and territories to ensure that every elder person in the community could age with dignity and in safety. However, the prime minister insisted that their priority was ensuring that they were supporting the provinces in their need to make sure that all seniors were protected right across the country in all those institutions.

Hon. Patty Hajdu introduced that Canada had the worst record of COVID-19 deaths in long-term care among 14 comparable countries, with over 80% of Canadian fatalities occurring in these facilities. The report from the armed forces showed appalling conditions, horrific care that was being given to the clients, and also the way that the staff conducted themselves. It was painfully clear that corporate profits were being put ahead of the well-being of seniors. The Minister of National Defence promised that the government was committed to working with the provinces and territories to ensure that every elder person in the community could age with dignity and in safety.

However, the opposition party argued that it was important to protect the employees who worked for the Liberals to ensure their re-election, yet the Liberal Party had raised more than $7 million since the last election.

He also promised that the fight against tax evasion was a priority for the government and they would continue to target companies and not innocent workers.

The members expressed concern about the economic difficulties faced by the UK due to the Brexit. The opposition party argued that the UK was a major trading partner for Canada and it was important for the Canadian government to ensure that the trade with the UK would continue to be normal while the UK went through the Brexit process. However, the opposition party also raised doubts about the stability of the relationship with the U.K.

Hon. Anita Anand (Minister of Public Services and Procurement) introduced that Canada was operating in a highly competitive global environment, and the reality was that we needed to make sure we had multiple complementary supply chains operating at the same time, which we had been doing in the past weeks and months, to ensure our front-line health care workers had the supplies they needed to keep Canadians safe. The opposition party also raised concerns about the availability of supplies, especially for essential goods, for agricultural products, for medical supplies. The Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food reassured the opposition party that they had multiple contracts in place for the procurement of N95 masks, including with 3M in the United States, whose masks were crossing the border weekly over the next month.
